722.title: Shibboleth (Judges 12:1–6)
722.hook: a word said differently becomes a death sentence
722.howItsDone: Jews read the shibboleth story in Judges 12 as part of the Former Prophets, often alongside Gideon's soft answer to the same tribe in Judges 8 as a study in how a quarrel between kin grows or cools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jephthah's vow and the daughter who came out dancing. Your line was rash vows cost. Did you take one breath before a yes? Today, Jephthah again, and a single word at a river. Day seven hundred twenty-two.

A ford on the Jordan, where the river runs shallow enough to wade. Men of Gilead are guarding it. A traveler comes down to the water and asks to cross. The guards ask him one question: are you an Ephraimite? He says no. So they ask him to say one word. Just one. "Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce it right." That's all it takes. One sound, a little off, and they seize him at the water's edge.
screen: `A GUARDED FORD.` → `ARE YOU AN EPHRAIMITE?` → `SAY SHIBBOLETH.`

segments.voice: How did it come to this? It starts with hurt pride. The men of Ephraim cross over to Jephthah after his victory, furious. Why didn't you call us to fight with you? We'll burn your house down over you. And here's what makes the story sharper. Ephraim made almost the same complaint once before, to Gideon, a few chapters back. Gideon answered softly. What have I done, compared with you? And their anger cooled. Jephthah answers with his own grievance, and then with war. Insults fly. The Gileadites win, and seize the fords so the Ephraimites can't get home. And at the river, the test is not what you believe, or what you've done. It's how your mouth makes one sound. The word itself is ordinary. Elsewhere in the Bible, shibboleth is an ear of grain, in Pharaoh's dream of full and thin ears, and in a psalm it's a flood of water rising. Nothing holy about it. Just a word with a sh at the front that some people said as s. These are not foreigners at the ford. Gilead and Ephraim are kin, tribes of one people, descended in the story from the same family. That's the grief of it. Brothers, divided by an accent, and a word for grain turned into a test of who's in and who's out.
screen: `EPHRAIM: WHY WEREN'T WE CALLED?` · `GIDEON ANSWERED SOFTLY; JEPHTHAH DIDN'T.` · `AN EAR OF GRAIN, A FLOOD.` · `KIN DIVIDED BY ONE SOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how accents divide people. Settle, and bring to mind a voice that sounds different from yours. An accent, a dialect, a way of saying one word. Notice whether the mind starts sorting it: from here, not from here, one of us, not. You don't have to fix that. Just watch. Then picture the person behind the voice, at their own kitchen table, saying the same word the way their mother did. The bell holds the time.
Shibboleth. An ordinary Hebrew word, an ear of grain, that became a test at a river crossing because some people said it differently. Today's word.
Your line: one word divides. Today, when you hear an accent or a word said differently, listen for the person before you sort them. Day seven hundred twenty-two.

what a scholar hears: the same word is an ear of grain in Pharaoh's dream (Genesis 41) and a flood of water in Psalm 69.

723.title: Samson's mother (Judges 13)
723.hook: the angel comes first to a woman whose name we never learn
723.howItsDone: Jews read Judges 13 as the haftarah for the Torah portion Naso, which contains the laws of the Nazirite, and rabbinic tradition pays close attention to Manoah's wife and gives her a name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shibboleth at the fords of the Jordan. Your line was one word divides. Did you listen for the person under an accent? Today, a new story, and it starts with a woman. Day seven hundred twenty-three.

She has no name. In the text she's the woman, his wife, Manoah's wife. She has no children. And one day an angel of the Lord appears, not to her husband, but to her. You will conceive and bear a son, he says. Drink no wine, eat nothing unclean, and no razor shall touch his head, for the child will be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he will begin to save Israel from the Philistines. The hero of the next chapters is Samson. But the story of Samson begins with her.
screen: `A WOMAN WITH NO NAME.` → `THE ANGEL COMES TO HER.` → `NO RAZOR ON HIS HEAD.`

segments.voice: She goes and tells her husband. Manoah prays: let the man of God come again, and teach us what to do. The prayer is answered, and the angel comes again, but again to her, sitting alone in the field. Manoah isn't there. She has to run and fetch him. When Manoah finally meets the angel, he asks for the rules for the child, and the angel's answer is mostly a pointer back to her: of all that I said unto the woman, let her beware. Manoah offers a meal, then asks the angel's name. The angel won't give it. A name withheld, in a story about a woman whose name we never learn. Then Manoah lays an offering on a rock, the flame goes up toward heaven, and the angel goes up in the flame. Manoah panics: we shall surely die, because we have seen God. And she is the one who reasons it through. "If the LORD were pleased to kill us, he would not have received a burnt offering and a meat offering at our hands." Nor would he have shown us all this, she says, or told us these things. She's calm, and she's right. The text leaves her nameless. The Talmud gives her one: Tzlelponit. Either way, the order of the story is plain. The angel came to her, twice. She heard it first, and she was the one who understood it.
screen: `MANOAH PRAYS: COME AGAIN.` · `AGAIN TO HER, ALONE IN THE FIELD.` · `THE ANGEL WON'T GIVE HIS NAME.` · `SHE REASONS THEM OUT OF FEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone nameless. Settle, and bring to mind someone whose name you never learned, who did something for you anyway. The stranger who gave directions. The driver who waited while you ran for the bus. The voice on the phone who sorted out a problem. Or someone in your own family line whose name has been lost. Hold them in mind for a few breaths. Thank them silently, without a name. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Samson's mother. Never named in the text, visited by the angel first and twice, and the one who talked her husband out of his fear. Today's word.
Your line: the angel came to her. Today, find out the name of one person you see often but have never asked, and use it. Day seven hundred twenty-three.

724.title: Delilah (Judges 16:4–21)
724.hook: strength given away a secret at a time
724.howItsDone: Jews read the Samson and Delilah chapters as part of the Former Prophets, and rabbinic commentary links Samson's strength to his Nazirite vow and asks why he gave his secret away.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samson's mother, and the angel who came to her twice. Your line was the angel came to her. Did you learn someone's name? Today, her son is grown, and he falls in love. Day seven hundred twenty-four.

In the valley of Sorek lives a woman named Delilah, and the lords of the Philistines come to her with an offer. Find out where Samson's great strength lies, and each of us will give you eleven hundred pieces of silver. The text says Samson loved her. It never says she loved him. And she doesn't hide what she's doing. She asks him straight out: tell me, I pray thee, wherein thy great strength lieth, and how you could be bound.
screen: `SILVER FROM THE PHILISTINE LORDS.` → `SAMSON LOVED HER.` → `TELL ME WHERE YOUR STRENGTH LIES.`

segments.voice: He lies to her. Bind me with fresh bowstrings, and I'll be weak. She does, with men lying in wait in the room, and cries: the Philistines are upon you, Samson. He snaps them like thread. Again: new ropes, never used. He snaps them too. The third time, listen to what he says. Weave the locks of my hair into the loom. He's still lying, but the lies are drifting toward the truth. Now it's about his hair. Then she presses him with a question: "How canst thou say, I love thee, when thine heart is not with me?" She pressed him daily with her words, the text says, until his soul was vexed unto death. And he tells her everything. No razor has come on my head; I've been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. Some readers hear the strength living not in the hair itself, but in the vow his mother was given, with the hair as its sign. She lulls him to sleep on her knees and calls a man to shave him. And when she cries out, the Philistines are upon you, he wakes and thinks, I'll go out as at other times and shake myself free. Then the line that hurts. He did not know that the Lord had departed from him. Nobody took his strength in one blow. He handed it over a little at a time, each lie a step closer to the truth.
screen: `BOWSTRINGS, THEN NEW ROPES.` · `THE THIRD LIE IS ABOUT HIS HAIR.` · `HOW CANST THOU SAY, I LOVE THEE?` · `HE DID NOT KNOW THE LORD HAD GONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard what makes you strong. Settle, and name one thing that holds you up. Sleep. A friendship. A daily prayer. Staying sober. A promise you keep. Hold it in mind. Then look honestly for the small ways you've been giving it away, a little at a time, because someone asked, or because saying no was tiring. Don't scold yourself. Just see it. And pick one small way to guard it this week. The bell holds the time.
Delilah. The woman of the valley of Sorek who asked again and again where Samson's strength lay, until he told her. Today's word.
Your line: guard your strength. Today, when you're pressed to give up the thing that keeps you steady, say no once, kindly and clearly. Day seven hundred twenty-four.

725.title: Once more (Judges 16:28–30)
725.hook: blind and chained, Samson prays for strength one last time
725.howItsDone: Jews read Samson's death in Judges 16 as part of the Former Prophets, often with the Mishnah's comment that Samson 'went after his eyes' beside the text.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Delilah, and a strength handed over a secret at a time. Your line was guard your strength. Did you say no once, kindly? Today, Samson with nothing left to guard. Day seven hundred twenty-five.

A prison house in Gaza. The Philistines have put out Samson's eyes and bound him in bronze chains, and set him to grind in the prison house. The man who once tore a young lion apart with his bare hands now grinds grain for the people who blinded him. And then, almost in passing, the text drops in one sentence: "Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven." Nobody in the prison notices. The reader does.
screen: `GAZA: BLIND, CHAINED, GRINDING.` → `THE HAIR BEGINS TO GROW.` → `NOBODY NOTICES.`

segments.voice: The lords of the Philistines gather for a great feast to their god Dagon, and they send for Samson to entertain them. The house is packed; people crowd the roof to watch. A boy leads him in by the hand. And Samson asks the boy something small: let me feel the pillars the house stands on, so I can lean on them. Then he prays. "O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God." It isn't the first time he has called on God; once before, dying of thirst after a battle, he cried out and water came. This time he asks for strength itself. Through all the chapters of lions and snapped ropes, the text never shows him asking for it. Now, blind and weak, he does. Remember me. Only this once. Notice too that the text doesn't clean up his prayer. He asks to be avenged for his two eyes. The rabbis noticed. The Mishnah says Samson went after his eyes, following what he saw and wanted, and so it was his eyes the Philistines took. The tradition keeps both truths: a man whose own choices brought him here, and a God who still hears him when he asks. He braces against the two middle pillars, and the house comes down, and he dies with them. He asked, and at the end, the strength came.
screen: `A FEAST FOR DAGON.` · `LET ME FEEL THE PILLARS.` · `REMEMBER ME, ONLY THIS ONCE.` · `HE WENT AFTER HIS EYES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for strength when weak. Settle. If there's a place where you're worn down right now, let yourself name it. Don't dress it up. Then, like Samson reaching for the pillars, find something to lean on: the chair under you, the floor, your own breath going in and out. Rest your weight there. If you pray, you can borrow two of his words: remember me. If you don't, just let yourself want strength without being ashamed of wanting it. The bell holds the time.
Once more. Samson's last prayer, blind and chained in Gaza: remember me, and strengthen me only this once. Today's word.
Your line: only this once. Today, when you're running on empty, ask for help once, plainly, from God or from someone near you. Day seven hundred twenty-five.

screen: `DAY 725 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: RIGHT IN HIS OWN EYES.`

726.title: Right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25)
726.hook: the book ends: "every man did that which was right in his own eyes"
726.howItsDone: Jews read the closing verse of Judges as the hinge into the books of Samuel, and commentators differ on whether it calls for a human king or laments a people who no longer answered to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samson at the pillars, asking for strength only this once. Your line was only this once. Did you ask for help when you were running low? Today, the book of Judges closes. Day seven hundred twenty-six.

Here is the last verse of the book of Judges: "In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did that which was right in his own eyes." That's it. No song, no victory, no wedding. The last chapters before it are hard to read: a private shrine with a hired priest, a tribe that carries off that shrine's idols and its priest, a crime in a city at night, and a war between the tribes that nearly wipes one of them out. And then that sentence, like a door closing.
screen: `NO SONG, NO VICTORY.` → `HARD CHAPTERS.` → `A DOOR CLOSING.`

segments.voice: The line isn't new. It has been coming back in those last chapters like a refrain: in those days there was no king in Israel. The text keeps saying it. And the full sentence, everyone doing what was right in his own eyes, stands at both ends of those chapters: as they open, and as the very last line. The phrase has a history. In Deuteronomy, Moses tells the people that in the land they will not do as they do now, every man whatever is right in his own eyes. Instead, the Torah says, do what is right and good in the eyes of the Lord. Same words, other eyes. And there's an echo inside Judges. When Samson first sees a Philistine woman and wants to marry her, he tells his father, get her for me, and in Hebrew what he says is: she is right in my eyes. The man who went after his eyes, in the book that ends with everyone doing what was right in their own. What does the closing line want? Readers differ. Some hear a call for a king, and the next book brings one. Others remember that Gideon refused a crown, saying the Lord shall rule over you, and they hear the problem as people with no one to answer to but themselves. Either way, the book ends on a warning about people who answer to no one but themselves. In its telling, a person's own eyes are real, and they matter, but they are not enough by themselves.
screen: `NO KING IN ISRAEL: A REFRAIN.` · `DEUTERONOMY: NOT IN YOUR OWN EYES.` · `SAMSON: SHE IS RIGHT IN MY EYES.` · `A KING, OR GOD AS KING?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one habit against more than your own eyes. Settle, and pick one habit you'd defend if anyone asked. How you spend the evening. How you talk when you're tired. How you spend money. Look at it through your own eyes first. Then through the eyes of someone it affects. Then, if you have one, through the eyes of your tradition. Just look. You don't have to change anything yet. The bell holds the time.
Right in his own eyes. The last line of the book of Judges, about a time when everyone answered only to themselves. Today's word.
screen: `RIGHT IN HIS OWN EYES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not just my own eyes. Today, before one decision, ask one other person how it looks to them. Tomorrow, the book of Samuel opens with a woman praying. Day seven hundred twenty-six.

727.title: Hannah's silent prayer (1 Samuel 1)
727.hook: a childless woman prays with moving lips; the priest thinks she's drunk
727.howItsDone: Jews read Hannah's story as a model of personal prayer, and the Talmud draws from her the way the silent standing prayer, the Amidah, is said: lips moving, voice too low for others to hear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last line of Judges: every man did what was right in his own eyes. Your line was not just my own eyes. Whose eyes did you borrow to check a habit? Today a new book opens, with one woman at a sanctuary. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

Every year a family travels up to Shiloh to bring an offering. Every year it goes the same way. Elkanah gives portions of the meat to his wife Peninnah and her children, and a double portion to his other wife, Hannah, whom he loves. Hannah has no children. And every year, the text says, Peninnah provokes her about it, until Hannah weeps and won't eat. Her husband tries. Why weepest thou, he asks; am I not better to thee than ten sons? It's a kind question, and it doesn't reach her. So after the meal she gets up, goes to the sanctuary, and stands before God. An old priest named Eli is sitting by the doorpost, watching.
screen: `EVERY YEAR, UP TO SHILOH.` → `PENINNAH PROVOKES HER.` → `ELI WATCHES FROM THE DOORPOST.`

segments.voice: What Eli sees is strange. A woman, her mouth moving, no sound coming out. The text says it plainly: "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." Eli decides she's drunk, and he says so: how long will you be drunken? Put away your wine. It's a sharp moment. The priest at the house of God looks at a woman praying with everything she has, and gets her completely wrong. Now listen to her answer. She doesn't storm off, and she doesn't swallow it. She corrects him, plainly. No, my lord, she says. I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit; I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but "poured out my soul before the LORD." Don't count me, she says, as a worthless woman. Poured out, the way you'd empty a jar. And Eli, to his credit, changes on the spot. He doesn't defend himself. He says, "Go in peace," and adds a blessing: may the God of Israel grant what you asked. Then comes a line that's easy to miss. Hannah goes her way, eats, and "her countenance was no more sad." Nothing has happened yet. There's no child, no promise beyond an old priest's blessing. The text doesn't explain the change. It only records it, right after she has said it all, fully, to God. The child comes later in the chapter, and she names him Samuel, saying she asked him of the Lord. That boy will matter in the chapters ahead. But it starts here, with a woman nobody could hear, and a priest who had to learn to listen.
screen: `LIPS MOVING, NO SOUND.` · `THE PRIEST GETS HER WRONG.` · `I POURED OUT MY SOUL.` · `HER FACE CHANGED BEFORE THE ANSWER.` · then, large: `SHE SPOKE IN HER HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray from the heart, or, if you don't pray, speak from it. Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Think of the thing you carry that you rarely say out loud, the one that comes back every year like the trip to Shiloh. Don't tidy it. Let your lips move if they want to, and keep your voice too low to hear. If you pray, pour it out to God the way Hannah did. If you don't, just let it be said, all of it, once. Then notice your face. The bell holds the time.
Hannah's silent prayer. A woman at Shiloh whose lips moved without sound, mistaken for drunk, who answered the priest and poured out her soul. Today's word.

Your line: she spoke in her heart. Today, if you catch yourself judging someone too fast, the way Eli did, do what he did next: change your mind out loud, and wish them well. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

728.title: Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:1–10)
728.hook: "He raiseth up the poor out of the dust"
728.howItsDone: Jews read Hannah's song as part of the book of Samuel, among the Prophets; by tradition her story is also read aloud in the synagogue on Rosh Hashanah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hannah at Shiloh, lips moving, no sound, and a priest who got her wrong. Your line was she spoke in her heart. Did you catch a quick judgment and change your mind? Today, the same woman, out loud. Day seven hundred twenty-eight.

Time has passed. The boy Hannah asked for has been born and weaned, and now she brings him back up to Shiloh, to the same priest, and leaves him there to serve, as she promised. Here is the woman whose voice nobody could hear last time. This time, the text gives us every word. The chapter opens, "And Hannah prayed, and said," and what comes out is not a thank-you note. It's a song about the whole world turning over. The mighty fall. The hungry eat. And in the middle of it, one line about where God goes looking for people: "He raiseth up the poor out of the dust."
screen: `THE BOY IS BROUGHT TO SHILOH.` → `THE QUIET WOMAN SINGS.` → `OUT OF THE DUST.`

segments.voice: Listen to how big the song gets, how fast. It starts with her: "My heart exulteth in the LORD." She has been mocked, every year, by someone with more. Now she says her mouth is enlarged over her enemies. Then, almost at once, it stops being about her. The bows of the mighty are broken, she sings, and those who stumbled are girded with strength. Those who were full hire themselves out for bread, and the hungry cease to hunger. "The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich; He bringeth low, He also lifteth up." One woman's answered prayer, and she reads in it a pattern for everyone. Then the line at the center. "He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, He lifteth up the needy from the dung-hill." Dust, and the dung-hill: the lowest places the song can name. And the next words say why: to set them among princes, to make them inherit a seat of honor. Not just rescued. Seated. A psalm says nearly the same words. And there's one more surprise at the end. Hannah's song closes with God giving strength to his king and exalting the horn of his anointed. A king. Two days ago, the book of Judges ended with the words: in those days there was no king in Israel. Hannah sings about a king who doesn't exist yet, and her son, the boy she just handed over, will be the one who anoints him. Some readers hear the whole book of Samuel folded up inside her song.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find someone in the dust. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who's low right now. Lonely, broke, ignored, ashamed, left out of the room. Picture where they're sitting. Then ask the song's question: what would it take, not just to help them up, but to give them a seat? A word of respect. A real invitation. A place at the table. Choose one small thing you could actually do this week. If you pray, you can hold Hannah's line for them: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust. The bell holds the time.

Hannah's song. The prayer Hannah sings at Shiloh when she gives her son to serve: the mighty fall, the low are raised and seated with princes. Today's word, closing a week that ran from the last judges to the first pages of Samuel.
Your line: raised from the dust. Today, lift someone out of the dust: do the small thing you chose, and if you can, give them a seat, not just a hand. Day seven hundred twenty-eight.
